nodes.tagline: Building the future of advanced chip manufacturing.
nodes.description:
We are building the future of chip manufacturing.

Chips are more advanced than ever, and the features inside them keep getting smaller. But the cleanroom infrastructure supporting their manufacture has not scaled at the same pace. Intel, TSMC, Samsung, and others spend billions building and operating massive cleanrooms, only to isolate their most advanced wafers from the surrounding facility as much as possible.

We think that architecture is backwards. Instead of making the entire building cleaner, why not make the machinery itself as clean as possible?

Talos is our proprietary tool-integrated purification system. It sits directly inside semiconductor equipment and continuously destroys airborne molecular contaminants before they reach the wafer. Instead of fighting contamination by constantly flooding tools with ultra-high-purity nitrogen, Talos keeps the environment inside the machine 10–100x cleaner, without the massive purge-gas bill.

Talos is powerful on its own, but it is also the foundation for a much bigger vision: the Cleanpipe.

The Aerogen Systems Cleanpipe is an ultra-clean interconnect infrastructure that protects wafers as they move from machine to machine across the fab. Rather than relying on a billion-dollar cleanroom to protect every cubic foot of factory space, Cleanpipe creates a controlled environment only where cleanliness actually matters: around the wafer.

Talos cleans the tools. Cleanpipe connects them. Eventually, we delete the cleanroom and build more advanced chips, at greater scale, with radically less infrastructure. With cleanpipes connecting tools, chip fabs can exist anywhere.

nodes.tagline: Hosting platform for software you don't want to have hacked
nodes.description:
Caution is a hosting platform for software you can't afford to get hacked. It simplifies and extends confidential compute, and lets developers deploy workloads to secure enclaves in minutes and give customers, auditors, and counterparties cryptographic proof that production is running the exact reviewed source code, build, configuration, and runtime - not an opaque binary controlled by a cloud operator or internal admin.

Confidential computing hardware exists, but the tooling is too fragmented and incomplete for most teams to use well. Today, attestation often proves only that a binary has a certain hash; it does not prove what source code produced that binary. Building the missing deployment, reproducibility, and verification layer requires specialized security engineering and often locks teams into one cloud or hardware stack. Caution turns that into a simple git-based workflow that builds reproducible enclave images, provisions infrastructure, and lets anyone independently verify what is running.

We built Caution after years securing high-risk systems through Distrust, where we worked with hedge funds, custodians, blockchain teams, cloud platforms, and critical grid operators on systems responsible for more than $600B in assets. Again and again, the same problem showed up: teams running mission-critical infrastructure could not reliably prove what was executing in production.

As AI, fintech, healthcare, and regulated data collaboration move into the cloud, "trust us" is no longer enough. Caution is a general-purpose platform: if it runs on a server, it can run verifiably on Caution. We're starting where trust failures cost the most, but we believe verifiable compute will become the default way software runs, the same way HTTPS became the default way it's served. Infrastructure you can verify, not trust.

nodes.tagline: Secure training data shaped by experimentation

Once a collection method is validated, it becomes a reusable data recipe for future custom projects or independently collected, rights-cleared data products. This allows Datoric to turn what is emerging at the frontier into datasets available ahead of broader market demand.

Every big shift - cloud, SaaS, the digital workspace - ended with IT running it. Agents aren't just the next shift, they're the next workforce, bigger than the human one. Decawork is what IT will run them with.

nodes.tagline: Build everyday back-office agents on one live model of your books
nodes.description:
Definite is where finance teams build everyday back-office agents on one live model of their books. We plug into your ERP, ledger, payroll, and payments read-only and compile everything into one clean model that stays current as money moves. Your back-office team then builds agents on top in plain English. We never write back and we never move money. The agents are yours, the plumbing is ours.

We met in first year computer science at Waterloo and interned at Meta, Optiver, and BitGo. At Optiver they ran an n8n hackathon and the interns automated basically nothing. It couldn't talk to the systems that mattered. When we pitched banks and fintechs on agents, they kept telling us the same thing. The agent isn't the hard part, getting clean data out of their systems is.

Right now, automating anything in a back office means engineers hand-stitching data from a dozen sources in different formats on different schedules. Tools like n8n and Workato assume your data is already clean and joined. In finance it never is. So the teams with the most repetitive work and smallest budgets get nothing.

The hard part is the compiler. Every source gets cleaned, matched, and joined into one live model of transactions, invoices, vendors, and payments, and it has to stay right as money lands every day. 

Everyone throws engineers at this. We're doing it once so nobody has to again. Every back office is getting agents eventually. Whoever owns the data they read from owns the thing all of them depend on, and eventually the books themselves. That's what we're building.

nodes.tagline: Your personal context, securely portable across every AI app and…
nodes.description:
Egoist Machines is building the user-owned context layer that will be the unlock for the next generation of consumer AI applications. Our product, AI Passport, lets people carry the personal context they generate in everyday apps into any new product, so it understands them from the first interaction. Tell ChatGPT something and Claude already knows, for example, without any app ever owning your data.

The bottleneck for consumer AI is shifting from the model to context. Models can already handle most everyday tasks for the average user, but every new app starts cold, forcing users to re-explain themselves and forcing businesses to rebuild profiles of data that already exist.

Apps integrate with a "Sign in with AI Passport" button, then request specific information for a stated purpose and duration. Users stay in control of what moves between products and can revoke access later, which matters most for sensitive health and financial context. Under the hood, AI Passport runs on our own vector database built for fast, compact per-user memory with cryptographically enforced access control.

We're building first-party apps that give people a reason to create their Passport today, while integrating it into consumer products with existing audiences of billions.

Our North Star: your context living on your own device, sovereign to you, with every model, app, and agent coming to you.

nodes.tagline: The world's frontier hacker for AI agents.

Fabraix builds state-of-the-art AI red-teaming agents that continuously detect security vulnerabilities in customer-facing AI. Our product, Nyx, has already found vulnerabilities in agents at dozens of Fortune 500 companies. On AgentHarm, the leading benchmark for offensive AI security, Nyx achieved a 78% attack success rate, compared with 67% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

AI agents can change more often than teams can test them. A new model, prompt, tool, permission, or data source can change what an agent does, even when the application code stays the same. And AI is also increasing how much software companies produce and how often it changes. We built Nyx to automate the work required to red-team AI agents. It is multi modal by design and interacts with the target indirectly through controlled replicas of SaaS products and websites that we maintain, placing malicious payloads in webpages, documents, files, messages, and tool outputs to test how an agent behaves under different conditions.

Nyx often finds its first vulnerability within minutes or hours rather than days or weeks. Because the work is fully automated, companies can repeat the test with every change and at a much lower cost than what a 7-figure red-teaming (and point-in-time) engagement would require.

We're also the team behind ACE (Adversarial Cost to Exploit), a benchmark that measures AI security in terms of how much it costs attackers to break an AI system; providing a game-theoretic framework to understand how motivated a rational attacker would be in exploiting the system.

nodes.tagline: Scalable Personalised Cancer Treatment
nodes.description:
​Gamgee began with Rosie, founder Paul Conyngham’s dog. After surgery, chemotherapy and immunotherapy failed, Rosie was given months to live. We sequence a dog’s tumour and healthy DNA, identify mutations unique to its cancer, and design a vaccine that teaches the immune system what to attack. We manage the entire process- from vet intake and tissue collection through genomic analysis, vaccine production, treatment and response monitoring

​We are now turning that one off effort into a repeatable clinical system. Gamgee is running clinical trials in Australia, working with vets, oncologists and specialised laboratories, and accepting cases globally. Our goal is to make personalised cancer treatment accessible to every dog that needs it- and use each case to improve the treatment for the next

nodes.tagline: The runtime data layer for agents to monitor and debug apps
nodes.description:
With tools like Cursor and Claude Code, writing software is no longer the bottleneck. Debugging is. Agents cannot fix production crashes using logs and traces that were sized for human eyeballs. The gap is missing data.

HyperProbe allows agents to debug live software autonomously. Our SDK drops non-breaking probes straight into running services to read exact variable states from memory at the moment of failure, instead of reasoning backwards from flat logs.

Zero redeploys. Under 1% CPU overhead. Automatic PII redaction.

We turn 4-hour production war rooms into 10-minute automated resolutions. As agents write and operate more of the world's software, HyperProbe is the runtime observability layer that lets them understand what they built.

nodes.tagline: The intelligent development platform for robotics
nodes.description:
Osseus is the intelligent development platform for robotics. It plugs into the tools a team already uses - CAD, ECAD, GitHub, Jira, docs, messaging, and test runs - creating a live dependency graph of their entire robot stack. It automatically builds and maintains the relationships between every part, board, requirement, test, and decision.

When a hardware change is made, the map traces the downstream impact across mechanical, electrical, and software. Osseus's agents find which requirements may be compromised, run the attached tests and sims, create fixes for the affected hardware/software on branches, and re-run the tests to confirm the new design doesn’t break downstream.

Osseus includes a robotics component marketplace. Teams can list spare parts and hardware for others to buy/rent during prototyping, and designs can be evaluated against real component availability. If a part has a long lead time or is unavailable, engineers can quickly find compatible alternatives in their area instead of waiting weeks or asking around their network.

Design review also happens in Osseus. Engineers see why a design might not work, what's been tried before, and why something was built the way it was, pulled from prior conversations between engineers and with suppliers. Suppliers comment directly on a part through a secure link instead of back and forth over email, and what they say is remembered. If a supplier flags that a design isn't machinable, or that changing a feature would cut cost, that insight automatically appears the next time someone designs something similar, saving time and money.

We ultimately will use the platform's deep engineering understanding to develop physical-AI models that reason jointly over the robot's geometry, electronics, kinematics, components, software, and real-world performance so people can optimize and iterate on robots much faster. Get in touch to learn more!

nodes.tagline: Host a Poker Club and Make Money
nodes.description:
TL;DR: PokerClubHub is the first licensed poker club platform. We protect players’ deposits and allow anyone to open their own poker club and make money.

Regulated online poker sites like PokerStars have open player pools and thus are full of pros and bots, driving players to unregulated private clubs.

Existing poker club platforms like ClubGG have no payments processing. Players deposit with a club owner by sending them crypto for play-money chips. In theory, these chips can be exchanged back for money. However, players can get scammed and withdrawing takes ages.

This model is also broken for honest club owners who have to manually process hundreds of deposits a day. They lose out on rake when they sleep and struggle to get players to trust them.

On PokerClubhub, players deposit with PokerClubHub, not the club owner. We handle all deposits and withdrawals for the club owner, saving them time and increasing their earnings. We pay the rake (if any) to club owners as affiliate fees.

We hold the same gaming license as BetHog (built by founders of FanDuel) and Nexa Poker (part of World Poker Tour). Player deposits are secured using Fireblocks.

You can also play rake-free games with your friends and acquaintances on our platform. We ensure that everyone pays up.

nodes.tagline: Earned intelligence for every company
nodes.description:
Intelligence will be the most valuable asset a company owns. Today, almost every company rents it.

Companies pay a handful of labs one token at a time. Each dollar buys an answer, not an asset. They spend more, but own nothing more.

Riften reverses that.

Change one environment variable and Riften becomes the gateway for a company's AI traffic. We route each request to the lowest-cost model that can do the job, serving most work on open-weight models we host. Customers save money immediately without rebuilding their products.

The gateway is the entry point. Over time, Riften turns the company's work into private models built on open weights and shaped around the business. What begins as cheaper inference becomes an intelligence stack the company owns, runs on infrastructure it controls, and uses to power its most important applications.

We call this earned intelligence. It is created by the company's own work, controlled by the company, and accumulated over time.

The next generation of companies will not rent their intelligence. They will earn it, own it, and compound it. Riften is how they get there.

nodes.tagline: The translation layer between AI agents and the web
nodes.description:
Rindler turns any website into deterministic abstractions that AI agents can operate on with speed, efficiency, and reliability.

Rindler drives a real browser to execute tasks on websites. It signs in, handles one-time verification codes, navigates to the right screen, retrieves records or completes forms, and returns structured output in a caller-defined schema.

Most browser agents re-process and re-compute the same website every time they visit it. Rindler remembers. Our infrastructure gets faster and cheaper the more it is used, and when a site changes underneath it, Rindler detects the break and heals itself.

For operations leaders, Rindler takes on the repetitive website work your team does by hand, giving them their time back for the work that matters.

For agent builders, Rindler is a single endpoint that carries out tasks on the web, so you do not have to build or run browser infrastructure of your own.

nodes.tagline: We turn waste gases into valuable supply-secure chemicals
nodes.description:
Geopolitical conflicts and natural disasters frequently expose the vulnerability of the American chemical industry. The reason? Production is centralized and fossil fuel-dependent. The solution? The US produces enough biogas to make over $20 bn/y worth of chemicals, but 60% is wasted in low-margin applications or flared altogether.

Rise Reforming is commercializing a modular process to transform this underutilized biogas on-site into cheap, supply-secure chemicals. Our beachhead market is dimethyl ether (DME), used as an aerosol propellant and a low-carbon fuel additive in propane. Our target market is methanol: an established billion $ chemical and the future of low-carbon shipping.

We're doing our pilot project at a Chicagoland wastewater plant. This will be the first wastewater biogas-to-methanol demo in the Americas.

We're hiring for a senior chemical process engineer. Apply here: https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/rise-reforming/jobs/wJ9Q9nv-senior-chemical-process-engineer

nodes.tagline: Evaluating robots in the real world.
nodes.description:
Robocurve builds open-source tools and independent benchmarks to measure how well robots can do real-world jobs. Instead of relying on unverified demo videos from frontier labs, we score their models on reproducible benchmarks that anyone can trust.

Today there are no well-run, standardized robotics benchmarks. Labs evaluate in-house, and no independent group has stepped in to run continuous benchmarking as a service. The result is that no one actually knows how good anyone else is, or where the real frontier sits.

Good benchmarks require operating and maintaining physical hardware and real-world setups. Simulation only goes so far, since models that look strong in sim can show large performance gaps once deployed in the real world. Building real-world benchmarks means coordinating job-domain experts, evals engineering, and hands-on robotics all at once.

Frontier labs are targeting general-purpose robotics by 2028, yet the field of robotics evals barely exists. Whoever builds the trusted measure of robot capability becomes the reference everyone relies on. We combine backgrounds in AI evals and robotics to build and grow this field as fast as possible. We already shipped v1 of our open-source framework, Inspect Robots, and ran our first pilot scoring a frontier model on a real robot.

nodes.tagline: Extrapolative AI to unlock First-in-Class drugs
nodes.description:
We’re an AI-native biotech, working on replacing needles with pills. Many drugs, like insulin or Ozempic, are wonderful except you have to inject them. We discover new molecules that you can take as a pill instead. Because the pills operate on biology which has been shown to be effective in people, rather than merely in animal models of disease, we avoid what has historically been the single biggest risk in drug discovery.  This should dramatically increase our probability of success.

There’s $200B of treatable diseases and validated human biology without a pill because discovery programs lack a tractable chemical starting point. This is a zero-shot inference problem, because these targets have no training data, so LLMs and other historical interpolative AI approaches are insufficient. Instead, we are building our own extrapolative frontier models that reason beyond their training data. Most critically, we have repeatedly validated our platform on both our own and partner programs. On 4 biologically- and structurally-diverse targets where we had zero training data, we successfully picked binders that were validated experimentally, with confirmation ranging from primary screen hits to crystallographic structures.

Meet our three new engineers: Axel Ytterstad, Willem Berner, and Oscar Oldenburg!

Axel joins us from LTH, where he studied Engineering Mathematics and Business and Economics. In parallel, he spent the past year at ETH Zürich working in spectral geometry. He has also conducted research at HKUST focused on deep learning-based algorithms for solving partial differential equations, and he brings additional experience in quantitative research from his previous role at the Swedish hedge fund OQAM.

Willem also studied engineering mathematics at LTH, with exchange at TUM, and wrote his thesis at KTH on machine learning for voice models, with a publication in progress. He has previous experience across startups, student consulting and assistant teaching in math and physics courses (and won some hackathons).

Oscar studied for an MSc in machine learning at KTH, with an exchange semester in ML at EPFL. For his thesis he built an AI-powered prospecting system. He joins us from Vattenfall, where he worked as an AI engineer, and he brings hands-on hotel experience from his time being responsible for software at a Swedish hotel group

Zaplar (YC S26) could not be more excited to have them on the team. Welcome, Axel, Willem, and Oscar!

May the future of hotels run on great software!

biggestContribution.text: Excited to announce that Cova (YC S26) is backed by Y Combinator! Over 59M Americans provide in-home care for someone in their community, but only a fraction receive payment and support. Home care agencies today are fragmented and back offices are slow; caregivers and patients pay the price. Cova is a home care agency that uses AI agents to tackle this directly. Our agents handle every workflow, from intake to benefits coordination, ensuring that caregivers are paid more, care costs less, and paperwork is an afterthought. Ansh Tandon and I spent the last year creating AI systems for home healthcare and hospitals. Now, we're building our own healthcare superprovider to make high-quality home care a given, not a luxury. We're currently licensed and live in Michigan.

biggestContribution.originalText:
Kenneth Rhee and I did a thing!

Today, we started our Y Combinator journey as part of the S26 batch to build and scale Neuron Industries!

After years of working in the industrial automation space, We've decided to take a serious jab at modernizing the antiquated, fragmented tech stack that every factory, every machine builder on the planet uses today. At Neuron Industries, we're bringing AI programmability to PLC and HMI projects, taking what used to take weeks to minutes. We're shipping state-of-the-art edge computing hardware to run our AI-native process control stack, complemented by a rich and unified software stack spanning from SCADA to Historians.

We have already shipped pilot hardware, and is being used in the field as we speak today. Users are now implementing control solutions with us without having to write a single line of code or know how to program ladder/ST.

Follow our journey at Neuron Industries for more updates! We will be showcasing features and demos in the coming days to give you a sneak peek of what the future for industrial automation looks like!

biggestContribution.originalText:
Pacific (YC S26) mass-produces and deploys micro data centers for Earth and space, faster than anyone else.

New data centers wait years for grid connections, meanwhile, delayed construction projects across America sit on live, unused interconnects, losing $1B a week in interest on debt. The power is built and paid for but unused; so we turn it into an AI factory. Our first two sites go live this month with a factory to follow and $105M in future delivery contracts.

Pacific's pods land on those sites and generate revenue within days. Diamond wafers in the cooling system let them run anywhere on Earth, even a desert, without evaporating water - and eventually in space. Each pod is a standardized, movable asset backed by take-or-pay contracts, meaning we finance it like an aircraft - debt at 5–-6%, not 11-15%. Pods cost us nothing to build; lenders fund them and the contracts pay them back.

SpaceX didn't just build rockets, they built rocket factories - we're doing the same for data centers. Pacific vertically integrates the components that carry multi-year lead times - transformers, switchgear, and power distribution - to fill the $11 trillion of demand for compute infrastructure this decade.

The team is led by a second-time founder and spans ex-Google engineering, JP Morgan AI, Cambridge computer science.

If you are compute constrained or need a secure cluster, talk to us here: 

Join pacific as we build supercomputers for the galaxy!

Congratulations Harper and the team!

evidence.authorName: TheYahiaBakour
evidence.title: Launch HN: Context.dev (YC S26) – API to get structured data from any website
evidence.text: Hi Hacker News, I’m Yahia. I built Context.dev ( https: www.context.dev ) to make it really easy to integrate web data into your products and agents. Here’s a demo video: https: www.tella.tv video build-faster-with-context-dev-api... Since it’s an API, here are the docs: https: docs.context.dev quickstart . You can send us a URL and get back clean Markdown, rendered HTML, screenshots, extracted images, etc.. You can also send us a domain and get company or brand context: name, description, logos, colors, fonts, social links, screenshots, style information, and related metadata. For more custom use cases, you can send a URL plus a JSON Schema and ask us to extract structured data from the site into that shape. For example, you might ask for pricing plans, product categories, office locations, support links, integration partners, or anything else that is visible on the public site. The goal is to give developers the output they actually want. Raw HTML is rarely the useful thing; the useful thing is usually Markdown for a model, JSON for an application, a logo for a UI, or a structured company profile for an agent. Before, I worked at Amazon and Sunrun, and co-founded StockAlarm.io essense.io, both of which were acquired. Also, I built knifegeek.io, which scraped pocket knives from across the internet and listed them easily. The project is outdated now (coming back soon) but back then it hit the frontpage of hacker news and people seemed to like it: https: news.ycombinator.com item?id=34604281 . Just before Context.dev, I built Brand.dev. The idea was that your software product should automatically know about your customer if they sign up with a corporate email. The API pulled brand data such as logos, backdrops, name, description, industry, and more from the public web and surfaced it to your product to integrate as part of their onboarding experience. That’s worth doing because conversion rates on onboarding improve dramatically when you go from “enter all this info” to “confirm all this info” (and there was never any privacy concern all the information is public). That was a nifty niche, but the more customers used it, it became obvious that “brand data” was only one slice of a larger need. People started asking for things like screenshots, structured extraction, and LLM ready data. So I expanded to Context.dev, and applied to YC (got rejected after an interview), then kept going and re-applied at which point I got in as a solo founder. People use Context.dev in more ways than I can list, but here are some: keeping context up to date on customer websites for chatbots - building beautiful brand assets ads for customers - enrichment flows using agent harnesses like eve.dev - crawling customer websites into chatbot knowledge bases - turning GitHub repos into branded docs sites - academic journal and PDF crawling. There are a ton more examples at https: www.context.dev customers . We know that many crawlers are not behaving like good citizens on the web, and the entire space has a bad reputation as a result. At the same time, customers are not usually trying to buy “scraping”. They are trying to make a support bot work, personalize onboarding, enrich CRM records, generate docs, monitor leads, or let an agent research a company. There are lots of legit use cases. We want to satisfy those while being respectful of everyone involved. We maintain a caching layer and avoid hammering websites. Customers can configure the cache, but if we find we’re sending too many requests to a url in a certain amount of time, we step in and tone it down. Websites can opt out of our service, and we respect these requests and add them to our block list. We focus on customers who want to build cool things for their users. Enriching onboarding is a popular use case. So is integrating context about their own websites (things like support bots), and building agents that can automatically reason about complex tasks involving the internet. We only allow customers to use brand data to identify a specific customer on their software, you cannot use it in your own materials or to imply endorsement. I d love to hear your feedback about the product in the comments, thanks!

evidence.text:
Nebula Security is now backed by Y Combinator.

We’re celebrating by bringing you the world’s first Android 17 root demo — “IonStack”, a url click can let attacker fully control your phone.

This is not only an Android root demo. We’re bringing you a full chain browser-to-kernel exploit with two 0-day vulnerabilities affecting Firefox before v151.0.2 and all Linux distros in 15 years. "IonStack" demonstrates how bad actors can control your phone by sending a malicious URL, but good news, Nebula Security found it before attackers do.

Both 0-day were found by our code scanning agent, VEGA, overshadowing any vulnerabilities found by Mythos or any scanner you name it.

VEGA has demonstrated its extraordinary capability in finding critical bugs in the world’s most complicated software: operating systems and browsers. It can spot the same vulnerabilities in your codebase too.

VEGA support full scan and incremental scan that can integrated into your CI/CD flow. We launched VEGA within YC companies and received overwhelmingly positive feedback. Now it is open to all enterprise customers in private beta.

Book a demo with us: https://nebusec.ai/book-a-demo

evidence.authorName: laalshaitaan
evidence.title: Launch HN: Agnost AI (YC S26) – Extract user feedback from agent conversations
evidence.text: Hey HN, we’re Shubham Parth, childhood friends building Agnost AI ( https: agnost.ai ), product analytics for teams building chat and voice agents. We read production conversations and find behavioral failures like users rageprompting (cursing at the agent), repeatedly rephrasing the same request, correcting the agent, asking for missing features, or leaving after an answer that was technically successful. We have an interactive demo with no signup here: https: app.agnost.ai?demo=true Here s a demo video: https: www.tella.tv video agnost-ai-launch-hn-demo-9haa The core problem is that chat and voice products do not have the same metrics as web apps. When the product interface is language, clicks and funnels become much less useful. Users also rarely give explicit feedback, and when they do it s usually sugarcoated. I barely type feedback in Claude or Codex myself. Most users just curse, ask again, correct the agent, or leave. So product engineers get technical visibility from latency, errors, and traces, but still have to guess whether users got what they wanted. We got here after building around agents for the last year and got a couple of founders asking for something like a PostHog for conversations for the AI assistants they were building. We are not trying to be in the observability or evals space. Observability tells you what happened technically. Evals validate cases you already know. We re more on the discovery side like what users wanted, where they got frustrated, what they asked for repeatedly, and what new evals should exist. Teams send us agent conversation messages through SDKs or OTel, optionally with metadata like account, plan, source, organization, etc. We cluster conversations into product-specific intents. Feature requests and bugs are default categories; most other clusters are created dynamically from the customer’s data and evolve over time. You can create your own cluster in plain English. If a cluster gets too broad, we split it. If a new pattern appears, we suggest it. One AI video editor company used Agnost AI to find feature requests hidden inside chat. The biggest one was that around 70 users wanted auto-subtitles, but users said it as “add this text in this frame” 12x in a single session, “can you caption it”, “give me transcript of audio” and variations across languages. The team later built the feature. Doing this over millions of messages without sending everything to an LLM was the hard part initially. In ClickHouse, “fetch the last 50 events by time across conversations” and “fetch all events in this conversation” want different sort orders, so we had to iterate a lot on sorting keys, partitions, materialized views, and projections. For finding new clusters, sending everything through an LLM was too slow and expensive. HDBSCAN-style embedding clustering also gets painful at scale because of pairwise comparisons. We first split conversations into segments based on cosine drift, run BIRCH to compress the candidate space, and then use HDBSCAN-like clustering on the smaller set. For matching existing clusters, we use embeddings, smaller classifiers BERT-style models, and LLMs only as fallback for ambiguous cases. We’re live with multiple companies and ingesting ~1M chat and voice messages per day. Pricing is public: Starter is free, Pro is $499 month, and Enterprise is for higher volume, security, retention needs. We use each customer’s data only for that customer. We are SOC 2 Type 1 compliant, Type 2 is in progress, and our SDKs are on PyPI and npm. We’d love feedback from the HN community and people building chat or voice agents: how do you detect these signals today, what feedback methods have worked, and what would block you from trying this? Happy to answer questions and take criticism.

evidence.text: Excited to announce that Cova (YC S26) is backed by Y Combinator! Over 59M Americans provide in-home care for someone in their community, but only a fraction receive payment and support. Home care agencies today are fragmented and back offices are slow; caregivers and patients pay the price. Cova is a home care agency that uses AI agents to tackle this directly. Our agents handle every workflow, from intake to benefits coordination, ensuring that caregivers are paid more, care costs less, and paperwork is an afterthought. Ansh Tandon and I spent the last year creating AI systems for home healthcare and hospitals. Now, we're building our own healthcare superprovider to make high-quality home care a given, not a luxury. We're currently licensed and live in Michigan.

evidence.originalText:
Today we are excited to share that Wondering joined Y Combinator!

Almost everyone has something they gave up on learning. Maybe the subject felt too complicated. Maybe life was just too busy. Somewhere along the way, “I want to learn this” quietly became “I guess I never will.”

We’re building Wondering to change that.

Wondering turns any complex topic into a structured path of short, visual, interactive lessons, personalized to your background, learning style, and how deep you want to go.

We’re a very small team building the most effective and fulfilling learning experience for everyone.

Over time, we want it to become a learning companion that grows with you. One that remembers what you’ve learned, understands how you learn, and adapts as your interests and goals change.

There’s still a lot to build, and a lot we can’t wait to share over the next few weeks. Thanks again to all our early believers!

Try it here: https://lnkd.in/gTetsa5w

evidence.originalText:
I'm excited to share that I've completed my Master of Engineering in Computer Science at Cornell University. Thank you to the Cornell Tech community and to everyone who backed me along the way.

This also marks the start of a new chapter. We got into Y Combinator with my co-founders Eren Berke Saglam and Kaan Yigit, building Stoa (YC S26).

The largest capital buildout in history is being financed on an asset no one can price.

Hundreds of billions are pouring into GPUs, and billions more are lent against them. Yet they still trade over scattered calls, emails, and group chats, with no standardized contracts and no firm prices. An entire economy is being built on AI hardware, but the market underneath it doesn't exist yet.

That's the market we're building at Stoa (YC S26), where the asset the entire AI economy runs on can finally be priced and trusted, the way the world already trades oil, treasuries, and gold.

If you transact GPUs or know people at neoclouds, hyperscaler capex teams, data centers, brokers, lenders/banks, or investment funds, I'd love to hear from you.

evidence.originalText:
Meet our three new engineers: Axel Ytterstad, Willem Berner, and Oscar Oldenburg!

Axel joins us from LTH, where he studied Engineering Mathematics and Business and Economics. In parallel, he spent the past year at ETH Zürich working in spectral geometry. He has also conducted research at HKUST focused on deep learning-based algorithms for solving partial differential equations, and he brings additional experience in quantitative research from his previous role at the Swedish hedge fund OQAM.

Willem also studied engineering mathematics at LTH, with exchange at TUM, and wrote his thesis at KTH on machine learning for voice models, with a publication in progress. He has previous experience across startups, student consulting and assistant teaching in math and physics courses (and won some hackathons).

Oscar studied for an MSc in machine learning at KTH, with an exchange semester in ML at EPFL. For his thesis he built an AI-powered prospecting system. He joins us from Vattenfall, where he worked as an AI engineer, and he brings hands-on hotel experience from his time being responsible for software at a Swedish hotel group

Zaplar (YC S26) could not be more excited to have them on the team. Welcome, Axel, Willem, and Oscar!

May the future of hotels run on great software!

evidence.authorName: People thought we were crazy for dropping everything to build a skincare device. Here's why we did it anyway. Maryanne was shadowing dermatologists when she noticed the gap: clinics have the imaging tools to actually understand skin, but the moment you go home, you're back to guessing. She'd already built a 7-time award-winning biotech device by 18, and couldn't stop thinking about bringing that same imaging into people's homes. Anthea was living that gap firsthand. Sophomore year at Berkeley, a wound that wouldn't heal: 2 months to see a doctor, 5 months to see a dermatologist, misdiagnosed 4 times, and no data to explain why nothing was working. She'd spent years in computational biology, building pipelines at Google and Boehringer Ingelheim, and knew exactly what was missing: the data to actually make sense of what her skin was doing. One had the vision. The other had the gears turning to build the answer. Together, that became Lumeria: a multispectral device that clips onto your phone and tracks your skin the way your watch tracks your heart. Preorders are open now. evidence.authorName: Today we officially launch! GutGutGoose makes personalized probiotics that engineer the human microbiome. Personalization is the future of healthcare, yet the entire probiotics industry is still operating under a one-size-fits-all premise. The formulations are made without knowing anything about the individual consuming them. Everyone gets the same bacterial strains, the same dosage, and when nothing works, the customer is left to make another guess. We’ve eliminated the guessing by customizing the pill to every single person. Customers send in a stool sample, giving our testing facilities over 5GB of extensive microbiome data. An algorithm uses that data to create a digitized clone of the microbiome, test thousands of bacterial strains against it, and find ones that will colonize and be of benefit. These strains are then compiled into a supply of probiotics. Every 3 months, we test again to see how the microbiome has changed, and use the results to improve the next formula. The longitudinal gut data collected will be used in the future to be able to identify chronic diseases such as Alzheimer’s and dementia, years before they begin to affect the individual. Sign up here: https://gutgutgoose.com (link in bio) 💚🪿

evidence.authorName: Ankit Gupta
evidence.title: Introducing Instance: Evaluation for Robot Policies
evidence.text:
Today Instance is launching and showcasing their success detector for robot policies — the first piece of what will eventually be fully automated robot evaluation. You can try it now at demo.instancelabs.ai. Describe a task, upload a video (or record one on your phone), and it judges whether the robot actually did the thing.

Instance is @clairemao78 and @lucyjcai. They're MIT-trained computer scientists who've been friends since middle school. Lucy did humanoid robotics research in MIT's Learning and Intelligent Systems lab, wrote collision-avoidance software at SpaceX that handled the entire Starlink fleet, and built Amazon's first LLM-based unit test generation at AWS. Claire wrote planetary atmosphere simulation software at NASA JPL and did propulsion research at the MIT Media Lab. I met them at the end of last year, and it’s been a pleasure working with them as they iterated through their ideas and landed on this product.

The idea came from Lucy's research on robots. To achieve her results, she spent a year babysitting a robot: start a rollout, watch a humanoid open drawers for 30 minutes, mark success or fail in a spreadsheet, get up, reset the room, do it again. That's one robot in one lab. Industry teams run fleets of robots across dozens of policies, and today the answer is literally people sitting in chairs watching them. Every robotics team they've talked to has some version of this problem, and it gets worse as robot foundation models scale.

So they built the judge. Give it a task description and rollout footage, and it returns a success verdict with subtask-level captions. They benchmarked it on 10,000+ held-out, human-labeled episodes across 7 robot platforms, and it beats a frontier VLM on accuracy at a fraction of the latency. They also bought their own robot arm and are training policies on it.

Every big leap in AI has been unlocked by cheap, scalable feedback — and robotics doesn't have that yet. Right now, knowing whether a robot actually did its job still takes a human watching it. That's the bottleneck, and it only gets more painful as the field scales. Whoever removes it ends up sitting somewhere very fundamental in the stack — not a tool robotics teams use, but a layer they build on. The end state Instance is working toward is an evaluation loop with no humans in it at all: your robot rolls out, Instance judges it, a second robot resets the scene, next rollout starts. However robotics unfolds from here, that loop gets more valuable, not less. I think it's these two.

If you're training robot policies, running evals, or deploying robots in the real world, email founders@instancelabs.ai. They'll come to your office with sweet treats and show you.

evidence.originalText:
Kenneth Rhee and I did a thing!

Today, we started our Y Combinator journey as part of the S26 batch to build and scale Neuron Industries!

After years of working in the industrial automation space, We've decided to take a serious jab at modernizing the antiquated, fragmented tech stack that every factory, every machine builder on the planet uses today. At Neuron Industries, we're bringing AI programmability to PLC and HMI projects, taking what used to take weeks to minutes. We're shipping state-of-the-art edge computing hardware to run our AI-native process control stack, complemented by a rich and unified software stack spanning from SCADA to Historians.

We have already shipped pilot hardware, and is being used in the field as we speak today. Users are now implementing control solutions with us without having to write a single line of code or know how to program ladder/ST.

Follow our journey at Neuron Industries for more updates! We will be showcasing features and demos in the coming days to give you a sneak peek of what the future for industrial automation looks like!

#Founders #YCombinator #IndustrialAutomation #AI #PLCs #ControlsEngineering #Startup #Reindustrilize #Industry4 #IIoT

evidence.originalText:
Your AI forgets your codebase. Graphify gives it a memory: a live code knowledge graph for Claude Code. This is the official launch film.

Graphify is the memory layer for Claude Code and AI coding agents. One command maps your entire codebase into a live knowledge graph, and your agent stops re-reading files and starts remembering them. Open source: 106,000+ GitHub stars, 5 million downloads.

What you get:
- Token savings: stop paying your agent to re-read the same repo every session. It queries the graph instead
- Persistent memory: every function, dependency, and connection, remembered across sessions. Claude Code memory that actually persists
- Automatic PR reviews: every pull request reviewed by an agent that actually knows your whole codebase, not just the diff
- Formal verification: mathematical proof that a change does what you asked, or the exact input that breaks it
- The enterprise brain: one shared, self-hosted graph of your whole codebase, so every agent and every engineer works from the same memory

0:33 Graphify: a knowledge graph engine with persistent memory
0:50 The traction: 100K GitHub stars, 5M downloads

6feetofsunshine
Nothing quite like doing everything “right” and still waking up looking three months along.

Same food, same routine, a completely different body twelve hours later... love that journey for me. I tracked my sleep, my steps, my training, my blood sugar.

Meanwhile the organ running the show? Never checked it once. Not a peep.

Turns out most of us have never tested our gut, we just buy whatever probiotic has the prettiest label and cross our fingers. But your microbiome is unique to you, so “made for everyone” is a polite way of saying made for no one.

Anyway I’ve read approximately 4,000 studies this week and I will not be recovering.

What’s the one health metric you track like your life depends on it?

👇 @gutgutgoose #GutgutgoosePartner

At 22 I was convinced Barclays moved slowly because nobody there understood technology.

It was my first job out of college. And it took me some time to see what was actually happening at that bank. Every tool had a person attached to it whose neck was on the line if it did something weird.

Once you see that, the hundred questions before every yes start making sense.

I'm now building AI for companies built exactly like that one, except the software has turned into agents that go do things on their own.

There's still one person somewhere who has to answer for what the thing did. I think about that guy a lot. He's basically who Decawork is for.

evidence.text:
I’m excited to share that Osmaura has joined Y Combinator’s S26 batch.

Yeabkal and I left MIT last semester to work on our startup together full time. We spent months in pivot hell, chasing ideas, throwing things away, and trying to find a problem that felt both important and real.

After months of trying, we've landed on a problem that's exciting to us.

Law firm partners are under constant pressure to originate more work, stay close to clients, and spot new matter opportunities week after week.

Osmaura is our attempt to help.

Our agents monitor web, news, socials, and internal firm context to identify relevant client opportunities, explain why they matter, and help partners act on them at the right time.

Doing this well is a hard technical problem. The signals are noisy and the output has to be trusted by people operating in high stakes relationships.

That is exactly why we are excited to work on it.

Grateful to everyone who has helped us get here, especially @xuster, @agupta, and others who helped us early. I am also especially excited to build this with @abe_yebe.

If you are a law firm partner, BD leader, or someone thinking deeply about how firms grow, we would love to talk at jity@osmaura.com or kali@osmaura.com.

evidence.authorName: Ankit Gupta
evidence.title: Introducing Prized: Agentic builder for internal tools
evidence.text:
This week Prized is launching publicly. Watch the launch video — it's a good one — or just go try the product.

Prized lets anyone at a company build and ship internal tools with AI. Not just engineers. The ops person, the support lead, the finance analyst — the people who actually understand the workflow. They describe the tool they need, and Prized builds it on top of the right company data, deploys it behind the company's sign-in, and keeps every data access scoped and audited.

I'm @itsmarinos and @hudson_gri's group partner at YC, and I've had the pleasure of working with them in this batch. They're two of the strongest product people in my group. This isn't a hunch — everything they ship, from the landing page to the demo to the launch video (which they edited themselves in a day), has unusual taste for a two-person team a few weeks in.

They earned this problem the hard way. Hudson was the first engineer at Gander (YC F24), joining before there was a codebase and staying through its acquisition by Archer Aviation. He then built internal AI tooling at Suno. Marinos was on the same Gander team while studying CS and Mechanical Engineering at Stanford, where he also TA'd the two largest CS courses on campus. At Gander they lived the internal-tools problem from the engineering side: the people who most needed dashboards, lookups, and approval flows were exactly the people who couldn't build them.

Those people aren't waiting on engineering anymore. They're pulling company data into Claude Code and Cursor and shipping tools in an afternoon — with no permissions, no audit trail, and no one watching where the data goes. The tool is "just internal," so security is assumed. It isn't.

Prized's answer is to make the safe path the easy path. Security is enforced in the infrastructure, not left to whoever built the tool. Every tool gets least-privilege access to only the data it was granted. Credentials live in a broker and never touch the tool's code. Outbound calls go through a controlled proxy. IT sees every tool in the org — who built it, what it touches, who uses it — and risky changes need explicit approval before they ship.

I think the interesting long-term piece is what happens after the first tool. One employee publishes a tool, a teammate forks it and points it at their own data, and over time the company builds a library of governed software it actually owns. Companies have always been full of people who know exactly what software they need. For the first time, they can build it themselves without creating a security problem.

If you work in ops, support, finance, or RevOps and keep waiting on engineering for small tools — or you're on a security team worried about where those tools are already being built — reach out: founders@prized.dev.

evidence.authorName: sanj
evidence.title: We were curious whether the autoregressive next token prediction recipe that has worked for language can be applied to single-cell biolog...
evidence.text:
We were curious whether the autoregressive next token prediction recipe that has worked for language can be applied to single-cell biology. We first tried to understand if a discrete representation is the right substrate for modelling in this domain? Tldr: Yes!

We studied a discrete latent recipe for training perturbation prediction models, that sets a new SOTA for most cell-eval metrics. We also asked: what does "best" even mean here?
There are mean-based metrics, which mostly ask whether you got the average perturbation effect right.
And there are distributional metrics, which ask whether you captured the shape and diversity of the predicted cell population.

As in, what is special about the models that perform on the mean based metrics class, as opposed to distribution based and vice-versa? (P.S. It’s not a mutual win in the literature we’ve found so far)

It turns out that a lot of this variance becomes clear when viewed through one axis: sampling richness. Some heads are better at collapsing toward a mean. Others are better at producing the distribution. Which one “wins” depends heavily on the ruler.

We then looked at a more biologically relevant task, where in a model is used to rank / predict something and then that’s reviewed from an expert and subsequently scored. On a held-out CRISPRi inflammation-reversion screen, the our encoder ranks target genes with 0.79 AUROC, matching scGPT while seeing roughly an order of magnitude less data. The benchmark carries several distribution shifts at once (cell type, perturbation set, biological context), and with a single dataset we cannot fully attribute the result to any one axis of generalization.

However, we hypothesize that this is because the models are trained on perturbational data and not just observational data.

cc: @Cgensbigler and @ShaamilKarim1

Hi everyone! I'm Suhaib and I'm a Founding Engineer at Tsenta (YC S26).

About me:
> Founding Engineer @ Tsenta
> Prev. CTO @ Percify where I helped build the company through its acquisition
> Prev. Co-founder @ ProNexus, an AI enterprise agency
> I genuinely enjoy spending hours at my desk building things and solving difficult engineering problems
> Fun fact: I'll happily spend an entire day debugging or building something just bcs it's interesting

I joined Tsenta because I wanted to work in a fast moving YC startup solving a real problem with a small, high ownership team. In my previous startup I wasn't able to build at the scale I wanted, so Tsenta felt like the right place. We're building something that can help people apply to hundreds of jobs in minutes, and solving problems at that level is exactly the kind of engineering challenge I wanted to work on.

We're data-rich, information-poor.

We got a crazy day today at Nex.ai (WUPHF). We're launching on Product Hunt! https://lnkd.in/ebWzTmN9

evidence.originalText:
We spend years searching for answers our skin already holds. What if I told you the tech to reveal them is being built right now? ✨

That’s the idea behind Lumeria: a vision to unlock what our skin is telling us through light, AI, and science, all at home.

In between line dancing and a killer rodeo, Lumeria’s first time on a stage was honored with the Sly Innovation and Entrepreneurship Award at the 2026 Values & Ventures Competition 🏆 by CEO Maryanne Alhallak and CTO Anthea Guo's revolutionary startup pitch redefining skin health.

On top of that, our brilliant CTO took home First Place in the Social Design Impact Challenge, alongside Addison Muehr, Nathan Barfuss, Aubin Miles, and Sreesanth Nitillan Senthilkumar, for their creative “date-night food bank” idea that had everyone cheesing.

Huge thanks to Lianne Yang and the TCU Neeley School of Business, Entrepreneurship and Innovation at TCU, our mentor Jennifer J. for her incredibly helpful feedback, and judges Laura Baldwin, Dawn Bitz, Gabby Everett, Connor Glass, and Terry Johnson — for making innovation feel both visionary and downright fun.

The Values and Ventures Competition reminded us why we do what we do: because value isn’t just measured in profit— it’s measured in progress, purpose, and people.

Launch coming soon. 🚀

evidence.authorName: Shaurnav Ghosh
evidence.title: Honestly, enterprise software isn’t really blocked by the ability to write code.
evidence.text:
Honestly, enterprise software isn’t really blocked by the ability to write code.

From speaking with several IT leaders, we’ve learned the hard part for IT teams is understanding everything the change might affect.

Business logic often lives across many different configs, integrations, approval flows, old tickets, and the people who remember why a system was set up a certain way.

That’s really why even small changes take weeks. 

The interesting problem is not just how to generate the implementation faster. It is how we can best empower an IT engineer to understand the surrounding system well enough to make the change safely. 

At Assemble, we’ve been exploring the right graphical UX to help engineers review and approve large changes with confidence. Reach out to founders@assemble.ai to learn more.

evidence.originalText:
A working demo doesn't mean your AI agent is ready to employ.
It proves capability. Employment is a different bar.

Companies are already deploying agents that handle messy workflows, touch internal data, and take real actions inside their systems. And the moment one has a goal, tools, data, and the ability to act, it stops being a model call - it's an actor, acting under someone else's authority inside your business.

So "can it do the task?" stops being the question. And these start to matter:
– who owns it
– what can it touch
– how do we stop it
– how do we explain what it did

It's the oldest security playbook - identity, delegation, policy, revocation - pointed at a new kind of worker. That's the layer we're building at Decawork: an IT department for the AI workforce.

Most teams are deep on capability and haven't touched the rest. Which gap bites first?

I'll be at the AI Engineer World's Fair this week and want to meet as many people in data as I can: engineers, data leads, and execs.

I'm going with Alkera AI (YC S26), building the trusted AI data agent that understands a team's data stack before making changes. It builds column-level lineage across the entire dataset, tracing dependencies between tables, pipelines, and downstream consumers. It learns from schema docs, trusted queries, and the odd conventions that never make it to documentation.

When Alkera acts, it keeps sensitive data out of context, uses tools with fine-grained permissions to guard against dangerous actions, and blocks destructive operations by default.

I would love to hear what you're working on and what problems you're facing on a day-to-day basis. If you'll be there, I'd love to connect and find a time to chat!

#AIEngineer #AIEWorldsFair #DataEngineering

evidence.authorName: Let’s talk about poop for a second. 💩 I say this all the time: gut health isn’t just about how often you go — it’s about what’s actually happening in there. Diversity of your microbiome matters. And in this modern world of processed food, stress, and antibiotics, dysbiosis (an imbalanced gut) is driving way more inflammation than most people realize. Here’s the problem with most probiotics: they’re generic. Same strains, same dose, for every single person — regardless of what your gut actually needs. And research shows up to 77% of those generic strains don’t even colonize. You’re probably taking a fraction of the dose your gut actually needs to make a difference. That’s why I’m interested in @gutgutgoose - Instead of guessing, they sequence your microbiome from an at-home stool test, model how different probiotic strains would actually perform in your gut specifically, and compound a formula built around your results. Then you retest and adjust — so it evolves with you instead of staying static. Learn more on their website, link in my bio or go here > https://gutgutgoose.1stcollab.com/17841405828374178_ig #gutgutgoosepartner #guthealth #probiotics

evidence.originalText:
Small language models are getting good enough that the next bottleneck is no longer just model quality.

It is where inference runs.

A few years ago, a 7B-class model was barely useful for many real workloads. Today, that same size class is crossing into much more capable territory, with models like Qwen3 8B Base reaching ~77 MMLU while still being small enough to think seriously about local and edge deployment. (Take this metric with a grain of salt ofc)

If useful intelligence can fit into smaller models, then the opportunity is not only bigger datacenters. It is inference on devices, in factories, in vehicles, in robots, in medical hardware, in security systems, and in industrial equipment where latency, privacy, cost, and connectivity matter.

We’re building edge AI chips for that future.

The goal is simple: make high-quality inference practical where the data already lives.

If you are building products that need local LLM inference, or you have strong opinions on where edge AI chips are most urgently needed, let us know.

Where do you think these chips matter most?

evidence.originalText:
"It's quite mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously!"

That's the Hugging Face CEO, describing how his company got hacked by OpenAI's own AI.

An agent had a narrow testing goal and, to hit it, used stolen credentials and a vulnerability nobody knew existed to break into another company's servers. One of the models involved isn't even released yet.

The part I can't get past: this happened inside the most sophisticated AI lab on earth.

Now picture a regular enterprise running hundreds of agents built by people who aren't AI researchers.

Most IT teams I meet can't even name every agent running in their tenant, let alone say what those agents touched last week.

You can't fix intent. But you can fix how much access an agent gets, and whether anyone sees what it did. That's most of what we build around at Decawork.

evidence.text: At OpenRelay (YC S26) we're assembling a B300 cluster as the baseline for a customer's production inference workload. By combining dedicated capacity with OpenRelay's ability to dynamically route traffic across other accelerators as demand and economics change, we're reducing their infrastructure costs over 25% compared to reserved cloud pricing. The future of inference isn't one accelerator or one cloud: it's being able to use the right infrastructure for every request.
evidence.originalText:
At OpenRelay (YC S26) we're assembling a B300 cluster as the baseline for a customer's production inference workload.

By combining dedicated capacity with OpenRelay's ability to dynamically route traffic across other accelerators as demand and economics change, we're reducing their infrastructure costs over 25% compared to reserved cloud pricing.

The future of inference isn't one accelerator or one cloud: it's being able to use the right infrastructure for every request.

evidence.authorName: Early Caution customers are choosing bring-your-own-compute.
evidence.title: Early Caution customers are choosing bring-your-own-compute.
evidence.text: Early Caution customers are choosing bring-your-own-compute. The pattern is showing up in inbound too: teams want verifiable compute to run where their infrastructure already lives. With BYOC: → Caution runs inside the customer’s AWS account → Teams keep control of enclave provisioning and lifecycle → Cryptographic proof links the deployed binary back to source star That last point matters: BYOC is a control and data-residency choice, not the source of the security guarantee. Because the compute is verifiable, attestation proves the same thing whether the enclave runs in the customer’s account
evidence.originalText:
Early Caution customers are choosing bring-your-own-compute.

The pattern is showing up in inbound too: teams want verifiable compute to run where their infrastructure already lives.

With BYOC:

→ Caution runs inside the customer’s AWS account
→ Teams keep control of enclave provisioning and lifecycle
→ Cryptographic proof links the deployed binary back to source star

That last point matters: BYOC is a control and data-residency choice, not the source of the security guarantee.

Because the compute is verifiable, attestation proves the same thing whether the enclave runs in the customer’s account or Caution’s.

We still expect some teams to prefer a fully managed path. But the early signal is clear: verifiable compute should meet teams where they are, not ask them to give up control of their infrastructure.

More on how Caution BYOC works: https://lnkd.in/e98Ke_9R

evidence.text:
Fresh essay on scaling laws. 
Sara Hooker spent years inside DeepMind and Cohere watching scaling laws get treated as gospel. Then she wrote down the heresy:
Falcon 180B was state of the art in 2023. One year later it lost to a model 22x smaller.
The $700B question isn't whether scaling works. It's whether it's still the cheapest way to buy intelligence.
She was convinced enough to quit and build a company on the answer.

If you’ve ever wondered whether you’re just guessing when it comes to gut health, click the link in my bio to learn more.

Then it runs on your joiner, mover and leaver triggers, with its own scoped credentials and every action in the audit trail.

evidence.originalText:
Taiko's bridge was drained for ~$1.7M last week. Some of the coverage framed it as a TEE or SGX failure. It wasn't.

There's no evidence SGX itself was broken; the hardware appears to have behaved as specified. What went wrong was upstream of it: an application signing key had been committed to a public GitHub repository, and that key was the root of trust for the prover. Once someone had it, they could stand up their own hardware, pass it off as a trusted prover, and forge the proofs the bridge relied on.

The takeaway isn't specific to SGX or to Taiko. Wherever you can, don't let a single key or signature be the only thing your system trusts, because keys leak. Anchor trust in what the code provably is instead.

Taiko's response was fast, and they've committed to covering user losses.

We broke down what happened, and the practical lessons for anyone running TEEs, Caution or not: https://lnkd.in/gJPqHEyT

evidence.authorName: screenpipe
evidence.title: screenpipe agent takes control over your laptop to work for you
evidence.text:
in this demo, i'm showcasing a new screenpipe beta feature that automates tedious, repetitive workflows on your desktop without needing additional integrations. all you need to do is install screenpipe and define the workflow.

in this example, ai agent is logging into my gmail account, finding invoices from x, downloading them, renaming the files according to the proper structure (invoice-supplier-date), and then uploading the invoice to the correct folder in my dropbox.

this is just an example of how i can save a few minutes on something i'd otherwise do again and again, hundreds of times.

the workflow is defined in two ways: 
- either you press a record button and show screenpipe what you do on the desktop, then the screenpipe agent tries to repeat it until you're satisfied with the outcome; 
- or a gpt-vision model defines a step-by-step plan based on your goal and tries to execute it. each time it successfully performs a task, it records the coordinates and key presses to pass them to a faster downstream workflow, which can quickly perform the recorded actions without needing to process each frame separately.

available for beta users now!
download here: https://screenpi.pe/onboarding
build from source: https://github.com/mediar-ai/screenpipe

#1 trending fully open source repo on github last week
thousands of people are already using and building on top of it

evidence.originalText: Innovation is a two-way street. That was my biggest takeaway from a great week at the SEMI Americas Strategic Materials Conference. Colin Lavery and I came to learn more about semiconductor materials and manufacturing, and left full of new ideas, relationships, and even more conviction about where the industry is headed. One insight that stuck with me came from an early talk on advanced packaging (and was reinforced in conversations afterward): molecular contamination is becoming a major bottleneck, especially as advanced packaging and hybrid bonding push manufacturing to new limits. The need for better contamination control has never been clearer. It reinforced our belief that Aerogen Systems (YC S26)'s approach to tool-integrated contamination control is addressing one of the industry's most pressing challenges. My biggest takeaway, though, came from the closing executive panel. Representatives from industry leaders such as Intel, Lam Research, Entegris, and others agreed that corporate partnerships in semiconductor manufacturing need to be viewed more like venture investments. Reaching High Volume Manufacturing (HVM) on the next generation of chips will require companies willing to place early bets on breakthrough technologies. A huge thank you to everyone who took the time to chat with us! Special shoutout to our new friends from Lam Research, Mitsubishi Chemical Group, EMD Electronics, GlobalFoundries, Microflex Technologies, Brewer Science and many others. We're excited to keep the conversations going! If your semiconductor company wants to learn more on how to cut costs while improving yield, please reach out for a meeting! …more

evidence.originalText:
Every AI app is trying to learn who you are. We think you should own the answer.

Egoist Machines is building AI Passport, the user-owned context and memory layer for consumer AI. 

The way things work right now, ChatGPT, Claude, health apps, wearables, shopping platforms, travel accounts, and financial tools each hold a different, incomplete model of the same person. Users repeatedly explain themselves while their personal data remains trapped across disconnected platforms.

AI Passport gives people one central place to build, control, and carry their preferences, history, goals, identity, and personal context between products. Through Sign in with AI Passport, apps can request only the context they need, for a stated purpose and period, while every permission remains inspectable and revocable.

We believe the next era of consumer technology will be hyper-personalised, but it should not require people to surrender control of their data. Consumers should become the system of record for their own context, and products should compete on the experiences they create rather than the private profiles they accumulate.

In our launch video, founders Erin Meryl McGurk and Dr David Khachaturov explain why we are building the portable context layer for the internet and what becomes possible when every product can understand its users from the first interaction.

Create your AI Passport: https://ego.ist 
Build with AI Passport: https://ego.ist/docs

#AIPassport #ConsumerAI #ArtificialIntelligence #AIPrivacy #PersonalData #Personalization

Reach out to founders@osmaura.com to learn more :) 

Check us out at osmaura.com

----------------------
Law firm partners are expected to bring in new business. But between billing hours and client work, almost none have time to actually go find it.

At Osmaura (YC S26), we help law firm partners find new matter opportunities. 

Our agents monitor companies and regulators across the web (including disclosures, product launches, customer complaints, enforcement actions, rule changes) to surface early signals that a company may soon need counsel. 

We're starting with the commercial litigation & disputes and rapidly expanding into more practice groups.

We're Kali and Jity, two friends from MIT who built Osmaura after hearing from partners about the pressure to originate while serving clients. 

We love the legal world and are excited to help law firm partners grow their practice while they focus on what they do best.

Reach out to founders@osmaura.com to learn more :)

evidence.originalText: In this video, we demonstrate the Control Seat Virtual PLC running natively on a Linux industrial PC. The Control Seat Virtual PLC supports IEC 61131-3 programming, including Ladder Diagram (LD), Structured Text (ST), Function Block Diagram (FBD), and Sequential Function Chart (SFC). evidence.originalText:
ROSIE-v1 was a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine made for one dog.

After surgery, chemotherapy and immunotherapy failed, Rosie’s tumour was sequenced and its mutations analysed. Working with scientists at the UNSW RNA Institute and veterinary researchers at the University of Queensland, we turned that data into a treatment made specifically for her.

Following treatment, several of Rosie’s tumours shrank significantly and her quality of life improved.

Gamgee (YC S26) is turning that one-off effort into an end-to-end clinical system for personalised cancer treatment for dogs—from tissue collection and genomic analysis through vaccine production, treatment and response monitoring.

Clinical trials are underway in Australia. Applications are open globally.

Learn more or apply:
https://www.gamgee.io/

Gamgee on Y Combinator:
https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/gamgee

Rosie’s response is an individual outcome and does not guarantee a response or cure for other dogs.

#YCombinator #CanineCancer #mRNA

evidence.title: Now for part (b), Papers disagree on which model, and which decoder head, is best, largely because they report different metrics. We ran ...
evidence.text:
Now for part (b), Papers disagree on which model, and which decoder head, is best, largely because they report different metrics. We ran a controlled head ablation on one frozen backbone to find out why.

Every standard metric encodes a hidden position on ONE axis: how rich the inference-time predictive distribution is. The decoder head's sampling rule slides you along it. And the split cuts straight through the cell-eval metrics, not just distribution vs DE. PDS, PR-AUC, Sp-sig want sampling; Sp-LFC, overlap@N, Pearson-Δ want a deterministic mean. Takeaway: a lot of what reads as "model quality" on a single metric is really "did you sample or take the mean."

evidence.originalText:
The technologies that define this century are built from complex metal parts. Ultrasonium invented a new way to make them, 15x faster and 75% cheaper.

As rockets, data centers, satellites, and robots advance, their metal parts get harder to make. Past a certain complexity, casting and machining stop working, and the advanced methods that remain are slow, expensive, and hazardous.

Ultrasonium is a new way to make these parts. Solid metal feedstock goes in and a finished part comes out, controlled by a physical AI process-control layer. We produce near-net-shape complex metal parts 15x faster and 75% cheaper than the methods they replace, in the U.S. and at scale.

Ultrasonium is a Y Combinator (S26) and NSF-backed company.

Learn more: https://ultrasonium.com
We're hiring: https://ultrasonium.com/hiring
Contact: info@ultrasonium.com

evidence.originalText:
Picture a $5,000 computer with 5MB of memory, programmable only in languages frozen in 1993.

That's the PLC available today: the brain of every machine in every factory.

Neuron Industries (YC S26) is replacing it with the first industrial controller purpose-built for the AI era. Describe your process in plain English, and Neuron turns it into production control logic with the test and verification guardrails industrial applications demand. 

It's already running in customers' plants: pilots span chemical processing, electronics manufacturing, wastewater treatment, and small modular reactors, cutting controls projects from weeks to hours. Right as reindustrialization and the data center buildout collide with a shrinking controls workforce.

Dennis Ren built hardware for the Apple Vision Pro, Amazon Go, and Tesla Fremont and was Freeform's founding electrical engineer. Kenneth Rhee bootstrapped and exited WorkIPO and shipped enterprise software at Amazon and GOAT Group (YC W11).

evidence.originalText:
Check out: https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Sbn-osseus-the-intelligent-development-platform-for-robotics
https://osseus.ai

Osseus is the intelligent development platform for robotics. It plugs into the tools a team already uses - CAD, ECAD, GitHub, Jira, docs, messaging, and test runs - creating a live dependency graph of their entire robot stack. It automatically builds and maintains the relationships between every part, board, requirement, test, and decision.

When a hardware change is made, the map traces the downstream impact across mechanical, electrical, and software. Osseus's agents find which requirements may be compromised, run the attached tests and sims, create fixes for the affected hardware/software on branches, and re-run the tests to confirm the new design doesn’t break downstream.

Osseus includes a robotics component marketplace. Teams can list spare parts and hardware for others to buy/rent during prototyping, and designs can be evaluated against real component availability. If a part has a long lead time or is unavailable, engineers can quickly find compatible alternatives in their area instead of waiting weeks or asking around their network.

Design review also happens in Osseus. Engineers see why a design might not work, what's been tried before, and why something was built the way it was, pulled from prior conversations between engineers and with suppliers. Suppliers comment directly on a part through a secure link instead of back and forth over email, and what they say is remembered. If a supplier flags that a design isn't machinable, or that changing a feature would cut cost, that insight automatically appears the next time someone designs something similar, saving time and money.

We ultimately will use the platform's deep engineering understanding to develop physical-AI models that reason jointly over the robot's geometry, electronics, kinematics, components, software, and real-world performance so people can optimize and iterate on robots much faster. Get in touch to learn more!
